title: Geometry-Controlled Polarization Photocurrents in Scalable PtSe2 Infrared Pixels
authors: Eunice Y. Paik, Owen A. Vail, Madaline R. Marland, William A. Beck, Antonio Llopis-Jepsen, Wendy L. Sarney, Jeffery H. Leach, Stefan Heiserer, Nikolas Dominik, Cormac Ó Coileáin, Paul B. Seifert, Georg S. Duesberg, Blair C. Connelly, George J. de Coster
abstract: Polarization-sensitive photodetectors provide multi-dimensional optical information beyond the capabilities of traditional intensity-based detectors. The noble metal dichalcogenide PtSe2 presents unique opportunities for tunable polarization detection due to its strong spin-orbit coupling, material stability, customizable broadband polarization responses, and direct compatibility with a wide range of substrates for back-end-of-line silicon integration. In this work, we demonstrate room-temperature near-infrared to mid-wavelength infrared polarization photoresponses using scalable, as-grown, wide-area PtSe2 films, and we show that the measured polarization response is reshaped by device geometry. Finite-element current-flow simulations reproduce the observed spatial redistribution of the polarization-sensitive response and localize the transverse polarization response near the pixel center. This geometry-enabled separation allows wavelength-dependent laser spot scans to distinguish symmetry-allowed photocurrents from contact-proximate, dichroism-mediated photothermal contributions. At near-infrared wavelengths, we observe spatial response that is consistent with linear-dichroic photothermoelectric currents, whereas mid-wavelength infrared measurements reveal a helicity-dependent photothermal contribution under oblique illumination. These results identify pixel boundary engineering as both a design lever and a diagnostic tool for scalable PtSe2 polarization-sensitive infrared pixels.
summary: This work demonstrates how the geometry of $	ext{PtSe}_2$ infrared pixels can be engineered to control and separate different polarization-dependent photocurrent mechanisms. By analyzing the spatial and spectral dependence of the measured current, the authors successfully distinguish intrinsic optical responses from artifacts caused by contact resistance or thermal effects. This provides a powerful, scalable platform for advanced IR sensing.
main_problem: The goal is to develop polarization-sensitive photodetectors for infrared (IR) imaging that can measure multi-dimensional optical information beyond simple intensity measurements.
main_result: The polarization response of $	ext{PtSe}_2$ pixels is strongly controlled by device geometry, allowing researchers to separate intrinsic optical photocurrents from extrinsic photothermal contributions.
method: The study combines experimental measurements of polarization-dependent photocurrents ($I(	heta)$) across various geometries (square, cloverleaf, bow-tie) with finite-element current-flow simulations.
model_or_system: The physical system is the noble metal dichalcogenide $	ext{PtSe}_2$, which exhibits strong spin-orbit coupling. The analysis models the photocurrent as a second-order nonlinear optical (NLO) response, incorporating photogalvanic and photothermoelectric effects.
key_observables: Polarization-dependent photocurrent coefficients ($C, L_2$), spatial redistribution of the response, and wavelength-dependent harmonic coefficients.
important_parameters: Operating wavelengths include near-infrared (976 nm), mid-infrared (1550 nm, 4600 nm), and the influence of device geometry (pixel shape).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the measured photocurrent contains contributions from intrinsic optical effects, photothermoelectric effects (PTE), and contact-related photothermal effects, which must be separated using geometry and wavelength dependence.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic device structures, polarization dependence ($I(	heta)$ vs. QWP angle), simulated current flow for different geometries, and spatial mapping of polarization-dependent coefficients ($C, L_2$) at various wavelengths.
paper_structure: The paper details the material characterization (structural/electronic), device fabrication, and then systematically analyzes the polarization-dependent photocurrent by comparing measurements from different geometries and varying excitation wavelengths to disentangle the underlying physical mechanisms (PGE, PTE, dichroism).
why_interesting: While primarily condensed matter/optics, the rigorous use of symmetry analysis, tensor formalism, and the separation of distinct physical contributions (e.g., optical vs. thermal) mirrors advanced techniques used in analyzing complex quantum response functions in open quantum systems.
